faqs.a: The first two thirds are not. The final building is dark and loud with a very large Indominus rex at close range, and then there is the drop. Children who have just cleared 42 inches frequently find the ending too much even when the dinosaurs were fine.

faqs.q: Is this the same as the Orlando version?
faqs.a: No. Orlando's Islands of Adventure has Jurassic World VelociCoaster and a separate river adventure; Hollywood's is the original 1996 river ride, rethemed in 2019 with newer animatronics and story. The Hollywood version has the better final animatronic; Orlando has the better coaster.

attractions.name: Revenge of the Mummy

scary.notes: This is the most frightening operating attraction at the park. It runs in total darkness, launches hard, reverses without warning, and includes a ceiling of fire you feel as heat on your face. There is a false ending that catches almost everyone the first time. Clearing 48 inches says nothing about whether a child is ready for it.

accessibility.notes: You must transfer out of a wheelchair or ECV into a coaster car with a lap restraint. All loose articles must go in the free lockers before the queue — enforcement at the platform is strict and there is no pocket that will hold anything through this ride.

attractions.summary: An indoor launched coaster in total darkness with fire, a reverse section and a false ending — the park's only real roller coaster.
description: Revenge of the Mummy opened on the Lower Lot in 2004 and is the only genuine roller coaster at Universal Studios Hollywood. It is an indoor, fully enclosed, electromagnetically launched coaster with a themed first act: you move slowly through Egyptian tomb sets, an animatronic Imhotep threatens the car, and then the launch takes the whole thing from a walking pace to full speed in about two seconds.

The Hollywood version is the shorter of the two Revenge of the Mummy coasters. Orlando's is longer, with more show scenes between the coaster sections. What Hollywood keeps is the essential structure: a slow scare-setup, a hard launch, a run through total darkness with a reverse segment and a fire effect, and a false ending that is one of the best-executed gags in any theme park.

The darkness is what makes it work. There is no reference point, no advance warning of a turn, and no lighting except the deliberate effects. Riders who are comfortable with much bigger outdoor coasters find this one genuinely disorienting, and that is the intended effect rather than a flaw.
experience: The queue runs through an Egyptian excavation site and into a tomb, well themed and mercifully indoors. Free lockers at the entrance are compulsory in practice — nothing survives this ride in a pocket.

The ride opens slowly. The car climbs through tomb chambers with scarab effects and an Imhotep animatronic, everything gets dark, and there is a moment of stillness that is the setup for what follows. Then the launch, which is abrupt and hard.

The coaster section runs in near-total darkness at speed, with a reverse segment, banked turns you cannot see coming, and a ceiling of fire above the track that you feel as real heat. It is short — the whole ride is about two minutes — and relentless while it lasts.

The false ending is the part people talk about afterward. The car comes to a stop, the lights come up, everything appears to be over, and it is not. Do not spoil it for anyone; it is the best moment on the ride.
tips: Use the free lockers. Enforcement is strict, there is nowhere to hold anything, and phones do not survive the launch in a lap.
Ride it first thing. The Lower Lot is close to empty in the first hour and this is often a walk-on before ten in the morning.
The single rider line is short and effective. In total darkness you cannot see who you are sitting with anyway.
Do not tell first-time riders about the ending. It is the best gag at the park and it only works once.
The fire effect above the track produces genuine heat, and the whole ride runs in true darkness with no reference points. Clearing 48 inches does not mean a child is ready for it.
attractions.bestTime: The first hour of the day, or the last hour before close when the Lower Lot empties out.
attractions.typicalWait: Usually 25 to 50 minutes from mid-morning; frequently under 15 in the first hour.

faqs.q: What is the height requirement for Revenge of the Mummy?
faqs.a: 48 inches, the tallest at Universal Studios Hollywood alongside Harry Potter and the Forbidden Journey. It is also the most intense ride here, and clearing the height says very little about whether a child will enjoy it.

faqs.q: Is Revenge of the Mummy scary?
faqs.a: It is the most frightening operating attraction at this park. The whole ride is in darkness, the launch is abrupt, there is a reverse section, a fire effect you feel as heat, and a false ending. Riders comfortable with big outdoor coasters still find it disorienting.

faqs.q: Does Revenge of the Mummy go upside down?
faqs.a: No. It has no inversions. It does have a backward section, sharp unlit turns and a hard launch, and the darkness makes all of it feel more extreme than the layout is on paper.

faqs.q: How does it compare to the Orlando version?
faqs.a: Hollywood's is the shorter of the two. Orlando's has more show scenes between the coaster sections and a longer track. The core — the launch, the darkness, the fire, the false ending — is the same, and Hollywood's is the more compact, more relentless ride of the two.

faqs.q: Do I need to use a locker?
faqs.a: Yes, in practice. Free lockers sit outside the queue and platform enforcement is strict. There is no safe place to hold a phone, a hat or a bag through the launch and the reverse section.

attractions.name: Transformers: The Ride-3D

scary.notes: Relentless rather than frightening. The vehicle moves fast and unpredictably through a dark building, the volume is the highest of any ride here, and there is a simulated fall from a great height near the end. Children are more likely to be overwhelmed by the noise and pace than scared by anything specific.

accessibility.notes: You must transfer out of a wheelchair or ECV into a twelve-seat vehicle with a lap restraint. The queue is indoors and air conditioned for most of its length. Almost all of the content is projected, so guests with significant vision loss get little beyond the motion and the sound.

attractions.summary: A motion-base dark ride through a Transformers battle, technically excellent, extremely loud, and hard on the inner ear.
description: Transformers: The Ride-3D opened on the Lower Lot in 2012, using the same ride system as Spider-Man at Islands of Adventure: a motion-base vehicle on a track, moving between enormous 3D screens with practical sets, effects and lighting between them. The premise is that you are riding an autonomous vehicle helping the Autobots protect an artifact from Megatron.

It is the most technically accomplished screen ride at the park, and by some distance the loudest thing on the property. The synchronization between the vehicle's motion and the projected action is genuinely good — there is a sequence where you appear to fall from the top of a building that works far better than it has any right to.

It is also unrelenting. Five minutes of continuous noise, motion and cutting, with almost no pause anywhere in it. People who enjoy that come off elated. People who do not come off needing to sit down, and the motion sickness rate here is second only to Forbidden Journey and The Simpsons Ride.
experience: The queue is themed as a NEST military base with briefing screens and equipment, entirely indoors and air conditioned, which is worth something on the Lower Lot in August. You are handed 3D glasses at the end.

The vehicle seats twelve across three rows and moves off immediately into the action. What follows is a continuous chase: the vehicle spins, tilts, drops and accelerates between screens, with practical fire, smoke and air effects filling the gaps.
The standout sequence is a simulated fall down the side of a building, where the motion base pitches the vehicle forward and the screen does the rest. It is the best-executed illusion at the park.
The middle row gives the least distorted 3D image. The back row takes the motion harder, which some riders prefer and some very much do not.
tips: Ride it in the first hour with the rest of the Lower Lot. Doing Jurassic World, Revenge of the Mummy and this back to back before 10am is the most efficient block of the day.
Do not stack this with The Simpsons Ride, Forbidden Journey or Minion Mayhem in the same hour. Those four together are how people lose an afternoon.
The middle row gives the cleanest 3D image and the least motion. Ask for it if you have a choice.
The single rider line is effective and, given that this ride is a wall of noise, you lose nothing by sitting apart.
This is the loudest attraction at Universal Studios Hollywood. If anyone in your group uses ear defenders, this is the ride to bring them for.
attractions.bestTime: The first hour of the day, alongside the other two Lower Lot rides.
attractions.typicalWait: Usually 30 to 60 minutes from mid-morning; often under 15 in the first hour.

faqs.q: What is the height requirement for Transformers: The Ride-3D?
faqs.a: 40 inches, the same as The Simpsons Ride, Despicable Me Minion Mayhem and Mario Kart: Bowser's Challenge. Forty inches is the threshold that decides how much of this park a family can do.

faqs.q: Does Transformers make you sick?
faqs.a: For susceptible riders, frequently. Five minutes of continuous motion synchronized to full-field 3D projection is a reliable trigger. It ranks behind Forbidden Journey and The Simpsons Ride at this park, which is not much of a reassurance.

faqs.q: Is Transformers scary for children?
faqs.a: More overwhelming than frightening. There is nothing designed to terrify, but the volume is the highest of any ride here, the pace never lets up, and there is a simulated fall from a great height. Younger children tend to find it too much rather than too scary.

faqs.q: Which row is best?
faqs.a: The middle row gives the cleanest 3D image and the least aggressive motion. The back row amplifies everything, which some riders prefer. The front sits close enough to the screens that the edges of the projection become noticeable.

faqs.q: Is it the same ride as the one in Orlando?
faqs.a: It was built to the same design, and Hollywood's opened first in 2012. If you have ridden one, you have effectively ridden the other. It shares its ride system with Spider-Man at Islands of Adventure, which is the more charming use of the same technology.

attractions.name: Raptor Encounter

scary.notes: The raptor is a puppet operated by performers and it behaves like a predator — it tracks movement, snaps, and lunges toward the guest being photographed. That is the entire point and it is very well done, which is also why a meaningful number of small children want nothing to do with it once they see it working.

accessibility.notes: Ground-level meeting with no transfer required and a short approach. Handlers control the pace and will keep the raptor at a distance if you ask, which is worth doing for a nervous child.

attractions.summary: A puppeteered velociraptor on the Lower Lot that behaves like an animal rather than a costume, and it is better than it sounds.
description: The Raptor Encounter is a character meeting on the Lower Lot near Jurassic World — The Ride, and it is the most convincing piece of live performance in the park after WaterWorld. The raptor is a full-body puppet worked by performers inside and out, with handlers in character managing the interaction as if the animal were genuinely dangerous.

What makes it work is that the raptor never breaks. It tracks movement across the queue, reacts to noise, snaps at handlers, and lunges at whoever is being photographed. Nothing about it behaves like a costumed character posing for pictures, and adults who queue for it out of curiosity come away impressed.

It is also the reason a number of small children refuse to go anywhere near it, which is a compliment to the puppeteering. Handlers will hold the animal at a distance if you ask, and a photograph from six feet back still looks like a photograph with a raptor.
tips: Ask the handlers to hold the raptor back if your child is nervous. They will, and the photograph still works from a few feet further away.
Do not wave your arms. The raptor tracks movement, and that is what triggers the lunge — which is fine if you were expecting it and less fine if you were not.
This is the best character meeting in the park, which surprises people who wrote it off as a photo stop.
Combine it with your one trip down to the Lower Lot rather than making a special journey. The escalators are not worth a photograph on their own.
attractions.bestTime: Whenever you are already on the Lower Lot for the rides; the queue is rarely long.
attractions.typicalWait: Usually 10 to 25 minutes.

attractions.name: Transformers Character Meetings

scary.notes: The costumes are very tall and the voices are processed and loud, which is enough to intimidate a small child at close range. Nothing about the interaction is aggressive and the performers are practiced at reading a nervous approach.

accessibility.notes: Ground-level meeting with no transfer required. The performers will come down to a seated guest's height, though the costumes limit how far they can bend.

attractions.summary: Optimus Prime and Bumblebee appear outside the Transformers ride, and the costumes are considerably better than they need to be.
description: Optimus Prime and Bumblebee appear on a rotating schedule outside the Transformers ride on the Lower Lot. The costumes are large, articulated and genuinely well built, with working lights and processed voices, and the performers stay in character throughout.

It is a straightforward photo stop rather than an experience, but the scale of the suits makes it a better one than most. Optimus Prime in particular is tall enough that the photographs work without any special framing.
Because it sits on the Lower Lot, the queue is almost always shorter than an equivalent character meeting up top. If you are already down here for the rides, it costs you ten minutes.
tips: Check the app for appearance times. The sets are short and the gaps between them are long.
Stand back a little for the photograph. The costumes are tall enough that a close shot cuts the head off.
The voices are loud and processed, which is enough to startle a small child on a first approach. Give them a moment before stepping in.
Fold this into your single trip to the Lower Lot rather than coming back down for it.
attractions.bestTime: Whenever you are already on the Lower Lot for the rides.
attractions.typicalWait: Usually 10 to 20 minutes.

attractions.name: The Starway

scary.notes: Not an attraction and nothing here is designed to affect anyone, but the escalators are long, steep and open, with a substantial drop visible beside them. Guests with a fear of heights find the descent genuinely uncomfortable, and it is worth knowing that before you are standing on it.

accessibility.notes: The escalators themselves are not usable by wheelchair or ECV guests, and are difficult with a loaded stroller. There is an accessible route between the two lots that avoids them — ask at Guest Relations on your way into the park and confirm with a team member at the top of the Starway, because it is not well signposted.

attractions.summary: Not an attraction: four long outdoor escalators between the Upper and Lower Lot, and the single biggest drain on your day here.
description: The Starway is a chain of four long outdoor escalators connecting the Upper Lot to the Lower Lot down the hillside. It is listed here because it behaves like an attraction in every way that matters to planning: it has a queue at peak times, it takes real minutes, and it is the reason people fail to see half of this park.

Four to five minutes each way when everything is running, longer when a section is out of service or the crowd backs up at the top. Coming up at the end of the night, on tired legs, it feels considerably longer than going down. There are landings between sections with views out over the Valley, which is a genuine consolation on the way up.

The planning consequence is simple and it is the most useful thing to know about Universal Studios Hollywood: go down once, do all three Lower Lot rides, and come back up once. Every additional round trip costs you close to fifteen minutes of walking you will not have budgeted for.
tips: Go down once and come up once. Plan the whole day around that and you will get more out of this park than any other single decision achieves.
There is an accessible route between the lots that does not use the escalators. Ask at Guest Relations on your way in — it is not signposted where you would expect.
Use the restrooms and buy drinks on the Upper Lot before you go down. The Lower Lot has far less of everything.
Do not come back up for lunch and go down again. Eat on the Lower Lot or wait until you are back up top.
If a section is out of service, expect the queue at the top to back up substantially. Check before committing to a late trip down.
attractions.bestTime: Once at the start of the day going down, and once when you are finished with the Lower Lot.
attractions.typicalWait: No queue most of the day; a few minutes at the top during peak arrival and departure periods.
